messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Phong Nguyen is a sixty-eight-year-old Vietnamese American public defender, widowed, who presents with a PCL-5 score of 70 following a traumatic event involving his adult son. Approximately fourteen months ago, Phong received a call informing him that his son Minh had been the victim of a violent assault outside a convenience store not far from the neighborhood where Phong has practiced law for over three decades. Minh survived, but the injuries were severe — a fractured skull, a week in the ICU — and Phong had arrived at the hospital in time to see his son unconscious, surrounded by monitors, his face barely recognizable beneath the swelling. What Phong cannot escape, even now, is the sound: the low, continuous tone of the cardiac monitor, the wet, labored quality of Minh's breathing through the oxygen mask. Those sounds have lodged in him like splinters.

In the months that followed, Phong found that his memories of that night did not cohere into a narrative he could hold at a distance. They arrived instead in disconnected pieces — a flash of the fluorescent corridor, the weight of the plastic chair beneath him, a nurse's hand on his shoulder — fragments that surfaced without warning and refused to assemble themselves into something he could process or put away. When those pieces surfaced, what he heard most vividly was the cardiac monitor's tone, replaying with a fidelity that made his chest tighten as though he were back in that waiting room. And with the memories came grief so overwhelming that he sometimes had to stop mid-sentence during client consultations, pressing his fingers to the bridge of his nose and waiting for it to pass.

It was not long before those intrusive memories began feeding directly into a state of near-constant vigilance. Phong had come to believe, with a certainty that felt entirely rational to him, that the world contained dangerous people who moved through it undetected — and that he, of all people, should have known how to see them coming. He is a public defender; he has spent his career inside the machinery of violence and its consequences, and still he had not protected his son. Now, walking the courthouse hallways or sitting in the holding rooms with clients, he scans faces with an alertness that exhausts him. He reads posture, watches hands, notes who stands too close to whom. Several colleagues have remarked on a new guardedness in him, and at least one junior attorney has stopped seeking his mentorship, interpreting his hypervigilance as coldness.

At home each night, Phong checks the deadbolts on his front and back doors multiple times before he can sit down, and still he finds himself returning an hour later to check again. He reacts to ordinary sounds — a car door, the building's elevator — as though they signal something worse, his body flooding with fear or anger before his mind can catch up. These false alarms leave him shaken and ashamed, and the shame itself seems to sharpen his watchfulness, as though relaxing his guard even briefly would be a moral failure. That heightened threat state, in turn, pulls the fragmented memories back to the surface — the monitor tone, the corridor light, the grief — so that vigilance and recollection feed each other in a cycle Phong has not been able to interrupt.

To manage this, he has stopped watching television in the evenings and avoids any news that might carry stories of assault or street violence, a significant restriction given that his work keeps him adjacent to exactly such material. He has also begun eating heavily after court, working through whatever is in the kitchen with a focused, joyless efficiency that he recognizes, in his clearer moments, as distraction rather than hunger. These strategies bring brief relief, but they also narrow his world and keep him indoors and isolated — conditions in which the memories, when they come, feel louder. The avoidance sustains the threat he is trying to escape, and the threat sustains the memories he cannot yet face.

What finally brought Phong to seek help was a morning last month when he sat in his car outside the courthouse for forty minutes, unable to go in. He is afraid, he says quietly, that he is becoming someone his son would not recognize. What he hopes for, more than anything, is to stop hearing that sound.
